newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Half of Swiss back Holocaust foundation - poll.
newsitem.headline: Half of Swiss back Holocaust foundation - poll.

text.p: Half of Swiss voters support a controversial government plan to launch a huge humanitarian foundation to aid the poor and persecuted, including survivors of the Holocaust, according to a newspaper poll on Saturday.

The plan to use seven billion Swiss francs in official gold reserves to start the foundation, which has drawn mainly right-wing criticism, was opposed by 33 percent of 600 people surveyed since it was unveiled on Wednesday.
The remaining 17 percent were undecided, according to the the daily Berner Zeitung that commissioned the poll.
The Swiss cabinet voiced relief at the first sign of broad popular support after two days of criticism led by far-right politicians suggested that the idea could be shot down in a referendum.

"This is a pleasant surprise. This result demonstrates a very widespread willingness among the Swiss people to support solidarity," government spokesman Achille Casanova told the newspaper about the poll.

President Arnold Koller proposed the "Swiss Foundation for Solidarity" this week in a bid to restore Switzerland's tarnished reputation after months of battering on the world stage by critics who said the country abused it neutrality to profit from World War Two.
The survey, which the newspaper said had a margin of error of four percent, was in sharp contrast to a telephone survey by the tabloid newspaper Blick that apeared on Friday.
Under the banner headline "No!", the tabloid said 90 percent of nearly 4,000 callers had denounced the plan as a waste of Swiss central bank gold reserves.
But the Blick survey was a telephone call-in poll, which pollsters say are not as accurate as random sampling surveys like the one for the Berne newspaper.

Opposition from the far-right is led by industrialist and parliament member Christoph Blocher, who said the cabinet had "lost its head" after Koller surpised a joint session of parliament with the plan.
The foundation proposal was endorsed by the Swiss Bankers Association, but one financier with ties to the central bank joined the public opposition on Friday.

Kurt Schildknecht, a member of the 40-member supervisory council of the Swiss National Bank (SNB), said using gold reserves for a political project would compromise the central bank's treasured independence.
"I am horrified," Schildknecht told Swiss television about the government proposal, adding he believed there could be indirect damage to the Swiss franc if the SNB's credibility was questioned.
SNB Chairman Hans Meyer has said the bank council approved the plan and that in any case it was up to parliament, not the council, to decide what to do with any profits from revaluing.

Berne has said the gold for the foundation would be available anyway under plans to revalue SNB gold reserves, which are now locked at a third to a quarter of market value by a 1971 law fixing their price at 4,595 francs per kg.

By revaluing the reserves at around 60 percent of market prices, the gold would be worth an additional 14 billion Swiss francs. Half of that gain would be given to the foundation as gold to be converted gradually into more profitable investments in order to provide the income for running the organisation.

Under the Swiss system of direct democracy, both the foundation and the revaluation of gold reserves will have to be approved by voters in a referendum which the government plans to schedule sometime in 1998.
